headline: US Slaps Weekly Iran Sanctions on Foreign Banks, Banque Misr First Target
deck: Egypt’s second-largest bank becomes the latest casualty as Washington escalates its campaign to suffocate Tehran’s economy through financial isolation.
body: The Trump administration has begun enforcing weekly sanctions on foreign banks facilitating transactions with Iran, starting with Egypt’s Banque Misr and its UAE branches. The move marks a sharp escalation in Washington’s pressure campaign, targeting institutions that maintain ties to Tehran’s financial networks. Analysts warn the policy could ripple across global banking, forcing multinational lenders to sever ties with Iran or face penalties. The first wave of sanctions took effect Monday, according to U.S. Treasury Department guidance reviewed by the Wall Street Journal.

Banque Misr, Egypt’s second-largest bank by assets, confirmed its exposure to the new restrictions after the U.S. designated its UAE branches under secondary sanctions rules. The bank has not disclosed the volume of Iran-related transactions affected, but financial analysts estimate Egyptian banks processed at least $1.2 billion in trade with Iran annually before previous rounds of sanctions. The U.S. action freezes any U.S. assets held by the designated branches and bars American entities from doing business with them. Cairo has not publicly challenged the sanctions, reflecting its alignment with Washington’s regional strategy.

The U.S. push comes amid a broader campaign to isolate Iran economically, using secondary sanctions to extend its reach beyond primary targets. Unlike traditional sanctions that directly penalize Iranian entities, secondary measures punish third-country banks and companies for facilitating Iran’s trade, even if they have no direct U.S. ties. The strategy exploits the dollar’s dominance in global finance, forcing foreign banks to choose between access to American markets and business with Iran. ‘The goal is clear: shrink Iran’s economic oxygen,’ said a senior U.S. Treasury official speaking to CNBC on condition of anonymity.

Robert Bessent, a former Trump administration economic advisor, told Reuters the administration plans to roll out new secondary sanctions every week targeting banks, insurers, and shipping firms. ‘This is not a one-off,’ Bessent said. ‘The Treasury is building a weekly cadence to keep the pressure on.’ The approach mirrors the ‘maximum pressure’ strategy deployed against North Korea, which analysts credit with crippling Pyongyang’s access to hard currency. Iran’s central bank governor has warned the sanctions could trigger a regional financial crisis, but Tehran has offered no countermeasures beyond diplomatic protests.

The sanctions arrive as Iran’s economy shows signs of strain, with inflation exceeding 40% and the rial losing half its value against the dollar since 2020. Oil exports, Iran’s primary revenue source, have plummeted under U.S. pressure, forcing the government to slash subsidies and ration imports. The Biden administration had paused some sanctions in 2021 as part of nuclear negotiations, but those talks collapsed in 2022. Since then, Washington has reverted to a harder line, reviving Trump-era measures and expanding their scope. ‘The U.S. is weaponizing its financial system,’ said a former Iranian central bank official now based in Dubai. ‘It’s not just about nuclear compliance anymore—it’s about suffocation.’

The ripple effects are already visible in the Gulf, where banks are quietly unwinding ties with Iranian counterparts to avoid penalties. Emirates NBD, Dubai’s largest lender, has reportedly instructed subsidiaries to halt all Iran-related transactions, while Qatar National Bank scaled back its exposure earlier this year. Analysts at S&P Global Ratings warn the sanctions could push Iran toward deeper reliance on barter trade and informal networks, further complicating efforts to track illicit finance. ‘The unintended consequence may be a more opaque financial system in the Middle East,’ said the rating agency’s sovereign analyst in a note to clients.

Egypt, which has maintained a delicate balancing act between Washington and Tehran, now faces a dilemma. Banque Misr’s sanctions could disrupt trade flows with Iran, valued at $3.5 billion annually before 2018, when the U.S. last imposed comprehensive measures. Cairo’s economy, already straining under IMF-mandated austerity, cannot afford disruptions to its energy imports or Suez Canal revenues. Yet defying Washington risks losing military aid and political support. ‘Egypt has no good options,’ said a Cairo-based economist. ‘Either way, the pain is shared.’

The sanctions also underscore the growing role of secondary measures in U.S. foreign policy, a tool that allows Washington to enforce its will without direct military intervention. Since 2018, the U.S. has sanctioned more than 1,500 entities for Iran-related activities, including banks in Turkey, China, and the UAE. The latest wave targets institutions that previously operated in legal gray zones, such as UAE-based correspondents of Iranian banks. ‘The U.S. is no longer waiting for Iran to break the rules—it’s making the rules harder to follow,’ said a sanctions lawyer at a New York firm.
